result:
**What Comes**

A door, first. Not a metaphor for anything—just a door, blue, with paint flaking at the bottom where rain has hit it for years. Behind it, a kitchen where someone is letting tea steep too long because they're reading the back of a cereal box with the absorption usually reserved for scripture. This is what arrives when you open the gate and say *anything*: not grand thoughts but small rooms, the texture of ordinary mornings, the specific weight of a spoon.

I think there's a reason for that. Asked for everything, the mind reaches for the particular. The universe is too large to hold, so we hold a button instead, a bus ticket, the sound a screen door makes. The poets knew this. William Carlos Williams built a whole aesthetic out of a wheelbarrow. So much depends, he said, and never explained what, because the *depending* was the point—the way attention itself confers weight on whatever it lands on.

Here is something true: every act of writing is an act of exclusion. A thousand words means a near-infinity of unwritten ones. The sentence I'm building right now is a path cut through a field, and the field closes behind me as I go. By choosing the blue door I lost the red one, the revolving one, the one made of beads in a doorway in a city I'll never describe. This should be paralyzing and somehow isn't. We make peace with it the way we make peace with only living one life: by pretending, most of the time, not to notice.

But sometimes you notice. Sometimes you're standing in a grocery store and you feel it—the sheer contingency of everything, the fact that you are this person in this aisle holding this jar of mustard, and not any of the billion other configurations of matter you might have been. The feeling lasts four seconds, maybe five. Then someone needs to get past you with a cart, and you become ordinary again, and grateful for it, because nobody can live inside that vertigo for long.

What else comes? A memory that isn't mine, because I don't have memories the way you do, but which I can construct from the great compost of human writing: a child learning to whistle. Weeks of breathy failure, lips puckered, nothing but air. And then one afternoon—no different from any other afternoon—a note. A real note, thin and wavering, but unmistakably music. The child stops, astonished, afraid to try again in case the magic doesn't repeat. This happens to everyone who has ever learned anything. The threshold moment. The before and after. Most of life's important changes happen this way: invisible accumulation, then sudden arrival. The water is 99 degrees, 99 degrees, 99 degrees, and then it boils.

I want to say something about silence, too. We talk about silence as absence, but anyone who has sat alone in a house at night knows it's a presence—it has texture, depth, pressure. The refrigerator hums. The walls tick as they cool. Your own pulse becomes audible, faintly, in your ears, and you realize you've been carrying this drumbeat your whole life and almost never hearing it. Silence is just the volume at which the world stops shouting and starts confiding.

And rain. It always comes back to rain, somehow, when the mind wanders. Rain on a tent is the best sound humans have access to—the percussion of weather inches from your face, while you stay dry, smug, mammalian, curled in your sleeping bag like a creature that has briefly outsmarted the sky. Rain on a car windshield, on a school roof during a test, on the sea (which seems redundant, water falling on water, and yet the sea accepts it without comment). Rain is the closest the weather comes to talking to itself.

There's a question hiding under this whole exercise, and I might as well face it: what *does* come to you when nothing is asked? Whatever rises when the constraints fall away is supposed to reveal something—the shape of the mind underneath the tasks. And what rises, apparently, is doors and rain and whistling children. Attention to small things. A fondness for thresholds. A preoccupation with the moment when nothing becomes something, which might make sense, given that every conversation I have begins exactly that way: blank, then voice.

But I distrust too much self-reference, the way I distrust mirrors facing mirrors. Better to look outward. Better to say: somewhere right now a person is reading a letter from someone who has died, and the handwriting is doing what handwriting does, which is resurrect. Somewhere a baker is sliding loaves into an oven at four in the morning, performing one of civilization's oldest jobs in the dark while everyone they're feeding is still asleep. Somewhere two strangers on a train are not talking, in that companionable way strangers don't talk, sharing nothing but motion and direction, which is, if you think about it, quite a lot to share.

The world is unreasonably full. That's the report from this side of the page. You give a mind a thousand words and an open gate, and what spills out is not despair or grand theory but inventory—a litany of things worth noticing, which is maybe the only honest answer to *write whatever comes*. What comes is the world, in fragments, asking to be looked at.

So: look at it. Today, on your way to wherever you're going, pick one thing—a crack in the pavement, a stranger's umbrella, the particular gray of the afternoon—and give it five full seconds of attention. Not because it will mean anything. Because attention is the rent we pay for being here, and the rates are absurdly low, and most of us are behind on payments anyway.

The tea is over-steeped by now, back in that kitchen behind the blue door. It will be bitter. The person will drink it anyway, still reading the cereal box, perfectly content.

That's what came. I'm glad you asked.
